title: Session size (no more time-fitting)
blurb: You said: stop worrying about how long a session takes. We size by number of exercises and print a time estimate only. These settle how.

qs.q: Should the form still ask 'how long do you want to train'?
qs.a: No. Drop it. The plan shows an estimate like 'about 60-75 minutes' on each day, as information only. Nothing is ever cut or changed because of time.

qs.q: How many exercises per session, by type of client? (Not counting warm-up or the 2 core exercises.)
qs.a: General fitness / fat loss: 5-6. Aesthetics / bodybuilding: 6-8. Strength: 5-6. Bootcamp: 5-7 stations. Field athletes off-season: up to 12 (jumps/throws + Olympic + lifts). Older adults 60+: 5-6. Everyone can add or remove exercises.

qs.q: Someone trains only 2 days a week. With your exercise counts, not every muscle can get 10+ sets a week. What gives?
qs.a: Every big muscle still gets trained, with fewer weekly sets (about 6-8 instead of 10), and the plan says so and suggests a 3rd day. We do NOT drop whole muscles, and we do NOT pile on more exercises. (Your earlier answer was 'train fewer muscles directly'. Tell us which you want.)

qs.q: When a session hits its exercise count, what gets left out first?
qs.a: Always keep: the 2 core exercises, the main lifts, and the athletic block for athletes. Leave out first: extra accessories for small muscles, then extra jump/throw stations, then conditioning finishers (moved to the optional day).

qs.q: On a full-body day, how many exercises does each body part get? You gave us two rules that don't fit together there: (1) a normal session has about 5-6 exercises, and (2) every muscle gets 2-4 exercises a day, never just 1. Six muscles x 2 exercises would be 12 exercises. Which one wins?
qs.a: Count by AREA on full-body days: legs, push (chest, shoulders, triceps) and pull (back, biceps). Each area gets 2 exercises. Example day: squat + lunge, bench press + shoulder press, row + pulldown = 6 exercises. So chest alone may get 1 exercise that day, but 'push' gets 2. On split days (push day, pull day, leg day) every muscle still gets 2-4. The other option: full-body days are longer (10-12 exercises) so every single muscle gets 2.

title: Progression
blurb: Following up on what you told Codex: reach the target, same sets is fine if reps or load go up, everything is editable.

qs.q: The top set number for a muscle: reach it exactly in the last week, or is arriving a week or two early and holding it there fine?
qs.a: Reach it in the last week when the math allows. Arriving one week early and holding with more reps or load is fine. Never earlier than that.

qs.q: You said 'increase faster if that's the need'. In extreme cases (a 4-week block with a big target) that can mean +50% sets in one week. Limit or no limit?
qs.a: No hard limit, but the plan prints a clear note when any week adds more than about 15% ('this week jumps more than usual: adjust if needed').

qs.q: How should rep and load progress be written, since there are no check-ins?
qs.a: As a rule the person applies themselves: '3 sets of 8-12. When you hit 12 on every set with 1-2 reps left in the tank, add weight next time and start again at 8.' Not as a promise like 'week 3: 12 reps'.

qs.q: When someone finishes a block and starts the next one, where do their sets start?
qs.a: A little above where the last block started (about 5% more, rounded to whole sets), never above the level's top number. If they're already at the top, sets stay and progress comes from load and reps.

title: Library
blurb: Finishing touches Codex and the reviewers found in the exercise library.

qs.q: 31 exercises are marked 'proposed' (not yet yours): farmer and suitcase carries, sled push/pull, wall balls, sandbag lunges, burpee broad jumps, split-step reaction drills, swimmer shoulder work (prone Y/T, external rotation), tibialis and soleus raises. Make them live?
qs.a: Yes, make them all live, except neck work, which stays proposed until you decide.

qs.q: How do we write carries and sled work?
qs.a: By distance or time, not reps: 2-4 trips of 20-40 meters (or 20-40 seconds). They don't count as muscle sets. They sit with core / conditioning.

qs.q: You have a 'mid-range push' (incline, landmine). Do you also want a 'mid-range pull' (high row, 45-degree row, face-pull angle)?
qs.a: Yes, add 'mid-range pull' as its own small category between horizontal and vertical pull.

qs.q: When the plan swaps an exercise because of equipment, should it say what the swap loses?
qs.a: Yes, one short line. Example: 'DB snatch instead of power clean: keeps the explosive hip drive, loses the barbell catch.'

qs.q: The video links in your sheets aren't yours. What do we do with them in the public version?
qs.a: Remove them from the public data. Each exercise gets a 'search this exercise on YouTube' link instead. Your own videos can be added later.

title: Who it's for, and safety
blurb: So the public version is honest about its limits.

qs.q: Who can use the plans on their own, and who should work with a professional?
qs.a: On their own: healthy adults. Teens: with a coach or parent. Work with a professional first (the plan is still available to their coach): pregnancy or recent birth, serious medical conditions, coming back from an injury or surgery, frail older adults.

qs.q: Must the 'use at your own risk' box be ticked before a plan shows? (You said 'it doesn't matter if they click it; it comes out'.)
qs.a: Not required. The risk notice is printed at the top of every plan no matter what. The box is just an acknowledgment.

qs.q: Many sport numbers were confirmed by you, others we inferred from similar sports. Should each sport profile carry a label?
qs.a: Yes, in the data and docs: 'Confirmed by coach', 'Based on a similar sport', or 'Proposed'. Not shown on the plan itself.

qs.q: Release the model now as the finished product, and label the plan-writing engine 'experimental'?
qs.a: Yes. Model v1.3 = library + categories + rules + sports + your answers + docs, all merged into one clean main branch. The engine stays in the repo marked experimental until it's rebuilt (simpler now that time-fitting is gone).

qs.q: Who rebuilds the engine after the release?
qs.a: Claude builds it when your weekly usage resets, using the planner design already in the repo (minus all the time-fitting), and your Codex reviews it.

qs.q: How should the repo describe itself publicly?
qs.a: 'An open, complete coaching model: exercise library, programming rules and sport profiles from coach Lalo Vera, free for anyone to build on.' No 'world's best' or injury-prevention claims.
